lines.text: The car dealership — or showroom — is where most new and many used cars are bought in Britain. Franchised dealerships represent specific manufacturers: a BMW dealer sells only BMW vehicles, with factory-trained technicians and genuine parts. Independent dealers sell multiple brands, often focusing on used cars at more competitive prices. The showroom floor displays the latest models — gleaming under spotlights, positioned on turntables, with specification sheets on the windscreen. A sales advisor greets customers, assesses their needs, and recommends suitable models. The test drive is a critical part of the buying process — typically a 20-to-30-minute route combining town driving, dual carriageway, and country roads. Financing options dominate modern car sales: PCP (Personal Contract Purchase) allows low monthly payments with a final 'balloon payment' to own the car outright, while HP (Hire Purchase) spreads the full cost equally. Leasing (PCH — Personal Contract Hire) means you never own the car but swap it for a new one every two or three years. Part-exchange — trading in your old car as partial payment — is standard practice. The dealer values your old vehicle and deducts its worth from the new car's price. Negotiation is expected: list prices are rarely the final price. 'What can you do on the price?' is the classic opening line. After-sales service — warranty support, servicing, and parts supply — keeps customers loyal to their dealership.

lines.text: UK consumer law (Consumer Rights Act 2015) gives strong protection when buying from dealers. If a car develops a fault within 30 days, you can reject it for a full refund. 'Not as described', 'not of satisfactory quality', and 'not fit for purpose' are the three legal tests.
